messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Public Transport: Bus riding, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 69, Linda had spent most of her adult life doing seasonal agricultural work, the kind of labor that organized her days by weather, harvest, and the routines of the same rural roads. She was married and had always thought of herself as practical, someone who endured hard things by keeping moving. The assault happened after a long workday when she was waiting for a bus ride home, tired and alone, and a man she did not know forced himself on her. In the months since, the details had not settled into the past. They returned suddenly and without warning, not as a story she could choose to tell, but as a memory that cut into the present with the same bodily jolt and shame. Bus riding became especially potent because the bus stop, the enclosed space, and the feeling of being trapped with strangers all belonged to what happened.

Afterward, Linda found that ordinary moments could set everything off. If she had to take public transport for work, or even saw a bus pull up along the road, the memory could come into her mind with such force that she felt she was right back there. Certain conversation topics—especially when other workers spoke casually about sex, safety, or men behaving badly—could bring the same sudden rush. When this happened, she tried to get through it the only ways that seemed to offer any relief: she drank in the evenings, sometimes took medication to dull herself, and increasingly kept away from other people. She also began mentally rehearsing worst case scenarios before leaving home, telling herself that if she imagined every possible danger she might be less helpless next time.

Those same triggers also changed the way she moved through the world. A bus passing her in town, a coworker starting the wrong kind of conversation, or a memory arriving out of nowhere could leave her scanning immediately, looking behind her to make sure no one was following. She had come to feel safe only in a very limited set of places—her house, one corner of the fields where she could see in every direction, her husband’s truck. Outside those zones, fear, anger, shame, and a sickened sense of exposure came on fast. What frightened her most was how quickly the feeling took over, as if the danger were not over at all but still waiting just outside her line of sight.

The triggers also fed the way she had started to think about herself. Each time she froze on a bus route or felt her stomach drop when a conversation turned, Linda took it as proof that she could not rely on herself anymore. She had once trusted her own judgment, and now she questioned whether she could keep herself safe even in ordinary situations. Around coworkers she increasingly felt set apart, as though everyone else still belonged to the everyday world and she had been pushed outside it. The sudden intrusions made her feel marked and isolated, different in a way she believed would never fully go away.

Over time, those beliefs hardened and began shaping what she did. Because she felt she could not rely on herself, she leaned more heavily on alcohol and pills to get through nights and to quiet herself before bus rides she could not avoid. Because she felt like an outsider, avoiding people began to seem sensible rather than sad; staying away spared her the strain of pretending to be normal. Worst case rehearsal also fit with that view of herself—if she was no longer the kind of person who could trust her instincts in the moment, then she felt she had to plan obsessively in advance for everything that might happen.

Those same beliefs made the triggers sharper. When a memory surfaced, it did not remain just a memory; it immediately confirmed for Linda that she was damaged, alone, and no longer capable of managing as she once had. Even overhearing certain topics at work could sting with more than recollection, because she was already primed to hear herself as separate from other people. In that state, she noticed buses more quickly, heard snippets of conversation more intensely, and seemed to brace for the memory before it even arrived.

Her constant vigilance tightened this further. Because she was always checking behind her and measuring where safety might still exist, the world became full of reminders. Bus stops, crowded aisles, and loose talk among workers stood out to her more than they once would have. The more she scanned for danger, the more easily the intrusive memory broke through. And the ways she coped kept narrowing her life. Avoiding people left her with fewer distractions and more room for the memory to intrude. Drinking and medication blurred the evenings but seemed to leave her more brittle the next day, while all the rehearsing of worst case scenarios kept her mind close to threat, so that even before dawn shifts in the fields she was already tense and looking over her shoulder.

She finally sought help after realizing how small her life had become. She had started refusing some transport-dependent work, withdrawing from coworkers, and relying on her husband for errands she once handled herself. What she fears most is that this is permanent—that she will remain an outsider in her own life, unable to trust herself, safe only in a shrinking set of places. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is to be able to ride where she needs to go, hear ordinary conversation without unraveling, and feel that the assault is no longer happening every day.
